                                                ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS

                                                                   YUTA KUSAKABE AND SHIN-ICHI MATSUMURA


                                                  Abstract. We prove that every weakly pseudoconvex Oka manifold admitting a posi-
                                                  tive line bundle is elliptic in the sense of Gromov, thereby proving Gromov’s ellipticity
                                                  conjecture.




arXiv:2610.12175v1 [math.CV] 8 Oct 2026
                                                     The proof establishes a cohomological construction of local sprays. Given a bundle
                                                  morphism φ : E → TX , we introduce quadratic φ-vector fields on E whose flows yield
                                                  local sprays with fibre derivative φ. Their existence is characterized by the vanishing of
                                                  the symmetrized φ-Atiyah class of E. This gives a local dominating spray on every weakly
                                                  pseudoconvex manifold admitting a positive line bundle, without any Oka assumption.
                                                     The positivity hypothesis is essential even for local existence: blow-ups at a single
                                                  point of complex tori of algebraic dimension zero, and Kummer surfaces of algebraic
                                                  dimension zero, admit no local dominating spray. The torus examples give compact
                                                  Kähler Oka manifolds that are not elliptic and show that ellipticity is not preserved under
                                                  blowing up, and that it is neither open nor closed in holomorphic families of compact
                                                  Oka manifolds. Combined with the work of Xie and Zhao, the Kummer examples yield
                                                  Oka K3 surfaces that are not elliptic.
                                                     Under the additional Oka assumption, we globalize the local dominating sprays con-
                                                  structed above. The proof combines Oka approximation with a gluing argument based
                                                  on weighted L2 estimates for the ¯  ∂-equation.

                                    1. Introduction
  We investigate the relation between the Oka property and ellipticity through the exis-
tence and globalization of local dominating sprays. Our main result is the following.
Theorem 1.1 (Gromov’s conjecture for weakly pseudoconvex manifolds). Every weakly
pseudoconvex Oka manifold admitting a positive line bundle is elliptic in the sense of Gro-
mov.
   A complex manifold X is called Oka if every continuous map from a Stein manifold to X
satisfies the homotopy principle; that is, it can be deformed into a holomorphic map, with
approximation and interpolation (see [8, Chap. 5] for the precise definition, and [7] and [8,
Sect. 5.4] for equivalent formulations). A complex manifold X is called elliptic if a vector
bundle p : E → X admits a dominating spray; that is, a holomorphic map s : E → X from
the total space of E such that s(0x ) = x and (ds)0x (Ex ) = TX,x for every x ∈ X.
   Gromov proved that every elliptic manifold is Oka [11] (see [8, Chap. 5] for a proof
and [8, Sect. 6.4] for examples). He stated, without proof, that the converse holds for
holomorphically convex manifolds admitting a positive line bundle [11, 3.2.A′′ ]. We refer
to this as Gromov’s conjecture. He also observed that the converse holds for Stein manifolds
[11, 3.2.A]. The converse fails without additional assumptions: the first author found Oka
manifolds that are not elliptic [14]. For instance, if n ≥ 2, the complement Cn \ K of a
compact polynomially convex set K is Oka [15, Theorem 1.6], whereas it is not elliptic if
n ≥ 3 and K has nonempty interior [2]. All these examples are noncompact. Recently,
Forstnerič and Lárusson settled the projective case [10]. Theorem 1.1 unifies and extends
these results, proving Gromov’s conjecture for weakly pseudoconvex manifolds admitting a
positive line bundle. The class of weakly pseudoconvex manifolds includes Stein, projective,
and holomorphically convex manifolds and arises naturally in several complex variables.
   The positivity hypothesis cannot be omitted, even among compact Kähler Oka mani-
folds. Our second main result shows that this obstruction already occurs at the level of
local dominating sprays.
Theorem 1.2 (Compact Kähler manifolds without local dominating sprays; see Exam-
ples 2.9 and 2.10).
    (1) Let T be a complex torus of algebraic dimension 0. Then the blow-up π : X :=
        Blt0 (T) → T at a point t0 ∈ T admits no local dominating spray.
    (2) Every Kummer surface X of algebraic dimension 0 admits no local dominating
        spray.
Here a local dominating spray is a dominating spray s : U → X defined only on an open
neighbourhood U of the zero section.
  The manifold X in the first assertion is Oka by [8, Corollary 6.4.13] (see also Buzzard’s
theorem on tame sets [5]). Thus, it gives the first example of a compact Kähler Oka
manifold that is not elliptic, answering a question of Forstnerič and Lárusson [10]. The
same example shows that ellipticity need not be preserved under blowing up, even among
compact Kähler manifolds. Moreover, varying the torus in holomorphic families shows that
                  ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                          3


ellipticity is neither an open nor a closed condition in holomorphic families of compact Oka
manifolds (Remark 2.12); recall that the Oka property itself is not closed in families [9].
   Combined with the work of Xie and Zhao [23], the second assertion yields Oka K3
surfaces that are not elliptic. It also gives another instance of the failure of openness:
there is a holomorphic family of Kummer surfaces whose central fibre is the elliptic Fermat
quartic, whereas all fibres outside a countable set of parameters are not elliptic.

  We divide the construction of dominating sprays in the proof of Theorem 1.1 into two
problems:
   (1) Local existence. When does a complex manifold X, without any Oka assumption,
       admit a vector bundle E → X carrying a local dominating spray?
   (2) Globalization. Given a local dominating spray on a weakly pseudoconvex Oka
       manifold, under what additional conditions can we construct a global dominating
       spray?
  A local dominating spray s : U → X on a vector bundle E → X induces a surjective
bundle morphism E → TX through its fibre derivative. This leads to the following question:
     • Given a surjective bundle morphism φ : E → TX , when can we integrate φ to a
       local spray on E whose fibre derivative is φ?
   We develop a cohomological approach to the local existence problem. For this purpose,
we introduce quadratic φ-vector fields on the total space of E (see Definition 2.2 and
Remark 2.3). Their flows integrate φ to a local spray, called an exponential φ-spray (see
Proposition 2.4).
   The existence of these vector fields is characterized by the following cohomological cri-
terion using the Atiyah class [3].

Theorem 1.3 (Cohomological criterion for quadratic φ-vector fields, Theorem 2.6). The
following conditions are equivalent:
   (1) The bundle E admits a quadratic φ-vector field.
   (2) The symmetrized φ-Atiyah class αφ (E) vanishes.

   Here αφ (E) is defined in terms of the Atiyah class a(E) of E (see Definition 2.5). The
theorem identifies the obstruction to constructing quadratic φ-vector fields and gives a
sufficient condition for integrating a prescribed bundle morphism into a local spray. When
φ is surjective, the resulting spray is dominating. Applying this criterion, we construct a
local dominating spray on every weakly pseudoconvex manifold admitting a positive line
bundle (Theorem 4.1). This construction does not require the Oka property.
  The Oka property enters in the globalization step, expressed by the following theorem.

Theorem 1.4. Let X be a weakly pseudoconvex Oka manifold, and let B → X be a positive
                          −1
line bundle such that KX     ⊗ B ⊗k admits a smooth Hermitian metric with semipositive
curvature for some integer k ≥ 0. If E = (B ∨ )⊕N admits, for some N ≥ 1, a local
dominating spray s, then E admits a global dominating spray that agrees with s to order 2
along the zero section. In particular, X is elliptic.
4                              Y. KUSAKABE AND S. MATSUMURA


   Here two holomorphic maps agree to order r along a submanifold A if, in local coor-
dinates on the target, all their partial derivatives of order < r agree at the points of A.
Theorem 1.4 follows from a jet extension theorem for maps from the total space of a neg-
ative vector bundle into an Oka manifold, with interpolation along the zero section (see
Theorem 3.1).
   In the projective case, Forstnerič and Lárusson used Stopar’s Oka principle on 1-convex
domains [20, Theorem 3.3] (cf. [18]). In our setting, the zero section may be noncompact,
so E need not be 1-convex and these results do not apply in general. The domination
off the zero section required in Theorem 3.1 is provided by Lemma 3.9, the analogue of
[10, Lemma 2.2]. The proof of Theorem 3.1 follows the local-to-global scheme of the Oka
principle for Stein sources [8, Chap. 5], with a gluing argument based on weighted L2
                   ¯
estimates for the ∂-equation  that preserves the prescribed jets along the zero section. Here
we treat the jet extension theorem only in the form needed to globalize sprays. The method
also extends to maps from general weakly pseudoconvex manifolds into Oka manifolds; we
will address this elsewhere.
   Organization. Section 2 treats local sprays: Section 2.1 establishes the cohomological
criterion, and Section 2.2 proves the nonexistence results above. Section 3 is devoted to
globalization: Section 3.1 proves a splitting lemma on the weakly pseudoconvex total space
of a negative bundle, and Section 3.2 proves Theorem 3.1. Section 4 proves Theorem 4.1
and Theorems 1.1 and 1.4.

                       2. Existence of local dominating sprays
2.1. Quadratic φ-vector fields and a cohomological integration criterion. In this
subsection, for a given bundle morphism φ : E → TX , we introduce quadratic φ-vector
fields and show, by considering their flows, that φ : E → TX can be integrated to local
sprays, called exponential φ-sprays (see Proposition 2.4). We also give a cohomological
criterion for the existence of quadratic φ-vector fields (see Theorem 2.6).
   Throughout this subsection, we work in the following setup.
Setup 2.1. Let X be a complex manifold of dimension n, let p : E → X be a vector bundle
of rank r, and let φ : E → TX be a bundle morphism, not necessarily surjective. We write
0x for the zero vector in Ex and 0X ⊂ E for the image of the zero section. For t ∈ C, let
mt : E → E denote fibrewise multiplication by t.
    We first define quadratic φ-vector fields.
Definition 2.2. A quadratic φ-vector field is a vector field Z on the total space of E
satisfying the following conditions:
       • dpv (Z(v)) = φx (v) (x ∈ X, v ∈ Ex ).
       • Z(tv) = t (dmt )v Z(v) (v ∈ E, t ∈ C).
Here (dmt )v : Tv E → Ttv E denotes the differential of mt at v ∈ E.
Remark 2.3. The definition is modelled on sprays in differential geometry in the sense
of Ambrose, Palais and Singer [1]. Indeed, for E = TX and φ = idTX , the first condition
                   ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                          5


says that Z is a second-order vector field, and the second one is the homogeneity condition
in [1]; thus a quadratic idTX -vector field is a spray on X in their sense. The exponential
φ-spray in Proposition 2.4 below corresponds to the exponential map of such a spray.
  We show that a quadratic φ-vector field on E integrates φ : E → TX to a local spray.
Proposition 2.4 (Integration of quadratic φ-vector fields). Every quadratic φ-vector field
Z on E is integrable; that is, there exist an open neighbourhood U ⊂ E of 0X and a
holomorphic map s : U → X such that
                               d
              s(0x ) = x,            s(λv) = φx (v)     (x ∈ X, v ∈ Ex ).
                              dλ λ=0
More precisely, such a map s : U → X is given by s = p ◦ FlZ             Z
                                                             1 , where Flt denotes the flow
of Z; we call it the exponential φ-spray of Z. In particular, if φ is surjective, then s is a
local dominating spray.

Proof. Step 1. Local expression of quadratic φ-vector fields. We first express the defining
conditions of quadratic φ-vector fields in local coordinates. Take an open set V ⊂ X
and a frame e = (e1 , . . . , er ) of E|V , regarded as a row vector. This frame defines the

  Since p(x, w) = x in this trivialization, we have dp(x,w) (c, d) = c. Thus, for v = e(x)w,
the first condition dpv (Z(v)) = φx (v) is equivalent to
(1)                                A(x, w) = φx (e(x)w).
In particular, the base component is uniquely determined by φ and is linear in w.

(dmt )(x,w) (c, d) = (c, td). Consequently, we obtain

fibre component to be homogeneous of degree two: one factor of t comes from the differ-
ential dmt , and the other from the scalar multiplying this differential. This homogeneity
is equivalent to the existence of a symmetric bilinear map γ(x) : Cr × Cr → Cr , depending
holomorphically on x, such that
(2)                               B(x, w) = −γ(x)(w, w).

Theorem 2.6 (Cohomological criterion for quadratic φ-vector fields). The following con-
ditions are equivalent:
    (1) The bundle E admits a quadratic φ-vector field.
    (2) The symmetrized φ-Atiyah class αφ (E) vanishes.
Proof. Every local trivialization of E yields a local quadratic φ-vector field. We show that
local quadratic φ-vector fields can be chosen so that they glue together precisely when a
cocycle representing αφ (E) is a coboundary.
Step 1. A cocycle representing αφ (E). Let {Vi } be a locally finite open cover of X by Stein
open sets, and let ei := (ei,1 , . . . , ei,r ) be a frame of E|Vi . Let {gij } denote the transition
matrices of E, defined by ei = ej gij . The fibre coordinates wi : E|Vi → Cr are the column
vectors defined by
                           v = ei (x) · wi (v)          (v ∈ Ex , x ∈ Vi ).

on every overlap.

for every v ∈ Ex . Multiplying this identity by the frame ej (x) turns it into an identity in

Since both sides are symmetric bilinear tensors, equality on all pairs (v, v) implies equality
on all pairs by polarization. This proves the gluing criterion.
Step 3. Conclusion. Suppose that (2) holds. Since {Cij } represents the zero class, there
exist sections Γi such that Γi − Γj = Cij . Let γi be their coefficient expressions in the
frames ei , and define Zi by (1) and (2). By Step 2, these vector fields glue together to a
vector field Z on E, which is a quadratic φ-vector field by its local expression. This proves
(1).
   Conversely, suppose that (1) holds, and let Z be a quadratic φ-vector field. Write Z
locally as in (1) and (2), and let Γi be the corresponding tensors. These local expressions
agree on overlaps since they come from the same global vector field. By Step 2, we have
Γi − Γj = Cij . Hence {Cij } is a coboundary, so αφ (E) = 0, which proves (2).             □
Corollary 2.7. If φ : E → TX is a surjective bundle morphism and the symmetrized φ-
Atiyah class αφ (E) vanishes, then there exists a local dominating spray s : U → X.
Proof. By Theorem 2.6, E admits a quadratic φ-vector field. Its exponential φ-spray is a
local spray with fibre derivative φ by Proposition 2.4. Since φ is surjective, this spray is
dominating.                                                                               □

The fourth summand consists of the mixed terms with values in L and is canonically iso-

is (1/2)a(L). Since a(L) ̸= 0 by deg L ̸= 0, it follows that αφ (E) ̸= 0. By Theorem 2.6, E
admits no quadratic φ-vector field, and hence no exponential φ-spray, although it admits
the global dominating spray defined above.
2.2. Examples admitting no local dominating spray. Theorem 4.1 shows that every
weakly pseudoconvex manifold admitting a positive line bundle has a local dominating
spray. However, a compact Kähler manifold without a positive line bundle need not admit
a local dominating spray. Thus the positivity hypothesis cannot be omitted in general.
Example 2.9 (Compact Kähler manifolds without local dominating sprays). Let T be a
complex torus of algebraic dimension zero, and let π : X := Blt0 (T) → T be the blow-up
at a point t0 ∈ T. Then X admits no local dominating spray.
Proof. After a translation of T, we may assume that t0 = 0. Write T = Cn /Λ; note
that n ≥ 2, since complex tori of dimension one are projective. Let Exc(π) := π −1 (0)
be the exceptional divisor. Suppose that a vector bundle p : E → X carries a local spray
s : U → X whose fibre derivative φ : E → TX is surjective. Set r := rank E ≥ n and
X ◦ := X \ Exc(π).
                   ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                         11


   We outline the argument. We consider a displacement δ defined by the dominating
spray s. The coefficients of the Taylor expansion of δ along the fibres impose a rank bound
along the fibres of an algebraic reduction of P(E) (see Step 4). On the other hand, we
construct a hypersurface S whose image s(S) is contained in Exc(π) (see Step 5). On S,
the displacement δ(v) depends only on the base point p(v), and its differential has rank n
in the same directions, which gives a contradiction (see Step 8).
Step 1. The displacement and its Taylor coefficients. Via the natural quotient map Cn →
T = Cn /Λ, we identify a small neighbourhood of the origin in T with a neighbourhood
of the origin in Cn , and we regard the points of this neighbourhood as vectors. Since
s(0x ) = x, we may shrink U to a fibrewise ball bundle such that π(s(v)) − π(p(v)) lies in
this origin chart for every v ∈ U . We define the displacement
                     δ(v) := π(s(v)) − π(p(v)) ∈ Cn                 (v ∈ U ⊂ E),
where the difference is expressed in the fixed origin coordinates. Since δ vanishes on the
zero section, its fibrewise Taylor expansion is
                              X                       1 dk
(8)                    δ(v) =     δk (v),   δk (v) :=            δ(tv).
                                                      k! dtk t=0
                             k≥1
The derivatives are taken componentwise in Cn . For every v ∈ Ex , the formula defining
δk (v) makes sense since tv ∈ U for sufficiently small t. Each δk is a homogeneous polynomial
of degree k on every fibre and corresponds to a global section of S k E ∨ ⊗ (X × Cn ). The
series in (8) converges locally uniformly on U .
Step 2. A coordinate map near the exceptional divisor. Choose ρ > 0 so small that
B2ρ ⊂ Cn lies in the origin chart fixed above, and regard Bρ as an open subset of T. Define
                                                            π
                           Q0 : N0 := π −1 (Bρ ) −−−−→ Bρ ⊂ Cn .
Then Q0 vanishes on Exc(π) and has differential of rank n on N0 \ Exc(π). For x, y ∈ N0 ,
the torus difference π(y) − π(x) is represented in the origin chart by Q0 (y) − Q0 (x).
Step 3. Fixing the algebraic parameter. Let q : P(E) → X be the bundle of lines in E, and
let ν : E \ 0X → P(E) be the natural projection, so that q ◦ ν = p. Choose an algebraic
reduction α : P(E) 99K Z, where Z is a smooth projective variety. Every meromorphic
function on P(E) is the pullback under α of a rational function on Z (see [22]). The
relevant maps are shown in the following diagram:

  We show that (π◦q, α) : P(E) 99K T×Z is a dominant meromorphic map. Let G ⊂ T×Z
be the closure of its image, obtained from the closure of its graph. It is an irreducible
12                             Y. KUSAKABE AND S. MATSUMURA


compact analytic subset surjecting onto both factors. Over a dense Zariski open subset
V ⊂ T, the projection G → T is flat, and its fibres Gt ⊂ Z have a common Hilbert
polynomial Q. They therefore define a meromorphic map T 99K HilbQ (Z). Since the
target is projective and a(T) = 0, this map is constant. Thus Gt = Z ′ for every t ∈ V , for
some fixed closed algebraic subset Z ′ ⊂ Z. Since G is irreducible, G ∩ (V × Z) is dense in
G. Taking closures, we obtain
                             G = G ∩ (V × Z) = V × Z ′ = T × Z.
   Hence the differential of (π ◦ q, α) is surjective at a general point of P(E). Since dπ is
an isomorphism on X ◦ , we obtain

at a general point [ℓ] ∈ P(E). Thus the base point in X can move in all n tangent directions
while the value of α remains fixed.

                    A := V × Dεr ⊂ U,        s(A) ⊂ N0 ,       S ∩ A ̸= ∅.
Replace S by a nonempty open set contained in A. The key point is that the same con-

                                      δ|S = −Q0 ◦ p|S .

Example 2.10 (Kummer surfaces without local dominating sprays). Let T = C2 /Λ be
a two-dimensional complex torus of algebraic dimension zero, and let X be its Kummer
surface. Then X admits no local dominating spray.

Proof. We note that T contains no curves, and hence no nontrivial subvarieties. Indeed,
let C ⊂ T be an irreducible curve. Since KT is trivial, the adjunction formula gives
C 2 = 2pa (C) − 2. As T contains no rational curves, we have pa (C) ≥ 1, and hence C 2 ≥ 0.
If C 2 > 0, then the line bundle OT (C) is big, and hence T is Moishezon. If C 2 = 0, then
pa (C) = 1 and C is a smooth elliptic curve, which is a translate of a one-dimensional
subtorus T′ ; then the quotient map T → T/T′ onto an elliptic curve yields nonconstant
meromorphic functions on T. In either case, a(T) ≥ 1, a contradiction.
    Let T[2] := (1/2)Λ/Λ be the set of the sixteen two-torsion points, and let π : T      e :=
BlT[2] T → T be the blow-up of T at these points. The involution y 7→ −y lifts to an
involution ιe of e
                 T. The quotient X = e T/eι is a K3 surface, and the quotient map τ : eT→X
                                                            −1
                                                                                S
is a double cover branched along the curves Γb := τ (π (b)). Set Γ := b∈T[2] Γb and
X ◦ := X \ Γ .
    Fix a ∈ T[2]. Suppose that a vector bundle p : E → X of rank r carries a local spray
s : U → X whose fibre derivative φ : E → TX is surjective at every point of Γa .
    As in Example 2.9, we use a displacement whose Taylor coefficients impose a rank bound
along the fibres of an algebraic reduction of P(E). We then construct a hypersurface S that
s maps into Γa . Passing to a branched double cover makes the displacement holomorphic
over S, where its differential has rank two in the same directions; this gives a contradiction.
Step 1. The squared displacement. Via the natural quotient map C2 → T, we identify a
small neighbourhood of the origin in T with a neighbourhood of the origin in C2 , and we
use this identification to regard small torus differences as vectors.
    The maps π and τ induce a natural unramified double cover τ ◦ : T◦ := T \ T[2] → X ◦ ,
whose two sheets are interchanged by y 7→ −y.
    Take a fibrewise ball bundle U ◦ ⊂ U ∩ p−1 (X ◦ ) such that s(U ◦ ) ⊂ X ◦ . For x ∈ X ◦ , we

Remark 2.11 (Oka K3 surfaces that are not elliptic, and non-openness of ellipticity).
Example 2.10, combined with the recent work of Xie and Zhao [23], has the following
consequences. Note that a two-dimensional complex torus T has algebraic dimension zero
if its Néron–Severi group vanishes. Indeed, if a(T) ≥ 1, then a nonconstant meromorphic
function on T has a nonzero polar divisor, whose class in NS(T) is nonzero since T is
Kähler.
(1) Oka K3 surfaces that are not elliptic. By [23, Theorem E (2)], there exist Oka Kummer
surfaces whose Néron–Severi lattice coincides with the Kummer lattice. Since the Picard
number of the Kummer surface of T equals ρ(T) + 16, the underlying torus T of such a
surface has Picard number zero. Since H 2 (T, Z) is torsion-free, NS(T) = 0, and hence T
has algebraic dimension zero. By Example 2.10, these Oka K3 surfaces are not elliptic.
(2) Ellipticity is not open in families. The Fermat quartic X0 ⊂ P3 is a Kummer sur-
face by a theorem of Mizukami (see [13, Appendix, Theorem A.1]) and it is Oka by [23,
Corollary 4.3]. Since X0 is projective, it is elliptic by [10] (or by Theorem 1.1). Let T0 be
a two-dimensional complex torus whose Kummer surface is X0 . Complex tori C2 /Λ are
parametrized by an open subset of the space of lattices, and those of positive algebraic
dimension, that is, those containing a curve, form a countable union of proper analytic
subsets of the parameter space. Hence there is a holomorphic family {Tt }t∈D of two-
dimensional complex tori over the unit disc D, with the given central fibre T0 , such that
Tt has algebraic dimension zero for every t outside a countable subset of D. Performing
the Kummer construction in this family (blowing up the sixteen sections of two-torsion
points and taking the quotient by the fibrewise involution), we obtain a holomorphic fam-
ily {Xt }t∈D of Kummer surfaces, that is, a proper holomorphic submersion with fibres Xt .
                   ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                           19


Its central fibre X0 is elliptic, whereas Xt is not elliptic for every t outside a countable
subset of D by Example 2.10. Therefore ellipticity is not an open condition in holomorphic
families of compact complex manifolds.
Remark 2.12 (Ellipticity is neither open nor closed in families of Oka manifolds). Ex-
ample 2.9 shows that ellipticity is neither an open nor a closed condition in holomorphic
families of compact Oka manifolds. For comparison, Forstnerič and Lárusson showed that
the Oka property itself is not closed in families [9]; in our families, every fibre is Oka.
   There is a holomorphic family {Tb }b∈B of two-dimensional complex tori over a connected
complex manifold B such that both the fibres that are projective and the fibres with
vanishing Néron–Severi group occur over dense subsets of B. Indeed, take the family of all
tori C2 /(I2 , b) Z4 with det(Im b) > 0; its period map identifies B with an open subset of the
period domain Q = {[σ] : σ 2 = 0, σ · σ̄ > 0} in P(H 2 (T, C)), where T is a fixed fibre (see
the proof of [19, Theorem II]), and NS(Tb ) consists of the integral classes orthogonal to σb .
For each nonzero class c, the locus {c · σ = 0} is a proper hypersurface of Q, so NS(Tb ) = 0
off countably many hypersurfaces. On the other hand, every σ ∈ Q is orthogonal to some
real class c with c2 > 0, since the orthogonal complement of the positive plane ⟨Re σ, Im σ⟩
has signature (1, 3); approximating c by rational classes shows that the loci {c· σ = 0} with
c rational and c2 > 0 are dense in Q, and over them Tb is projective [4, Theorem IV.6.2].
   Blowing up the zero section, we obtain a holomorphic family {Xb }b∈B , where Xb is the
blow-up of Tb at a point. Every Xb is Oka by [8, Corollary 6.4.13]. If Tb is projective, then
so is Xb , and hence Xb is elliptic by [10] (or by Theorem 1.1). If NS(Tb ) = 0, then Tb has
algebraic dimension zero (Remark 2.11), and hence Xb is not elliptic by Example 2.9. Thus
both the elliptic and the non-elliptic fibres occur over dense subsets of B, so ellipticity is
neither open nor closed in this family.

                          3. Globalization of local sprays
  Let f : U → Y be a holomorphic map between complex manifolds. A product spray with
core f is a holomorphic map H : U × P → Y such that H(·, 0) = f , where P is a ball
centred at 0 in some CM ; thus a product spray is a local spray over f on the trivial bundle
U × CM that is defined on U × P . It is said to be dominating over S ⊂ U if ∂ζ H(x, ζ)
maps onto TY,H(x,ζ) for all x ∈ S and ζ ∈ P . Such maps are called sprays of maps in [8,
Chap. 5].
Theorem 3.1. Let X be a weakly pseudoconvex manifold with a Kähler form ωX , and let
E → X be a vector bundle of rank N ≥ 1 with a Hermitian metric. Assume that, for some
                               −1
smooth Hermitian metric on KX     and some constant c ≥ 0,
           √
          ⟨ −1ΘE (v, v̄)ξ, ξ⟩ ≤ −ωX (v, v̄) |ξ|2   (v ∈ TX,x , ξ ∈ Ex , x ∈ X),
(15)                         √        −1
                               −1Θ(KX     ⊗ det E) ≥ −c ωX .
We identify E with its total space and let A be its zero section. Let Y be an Oka manifold,
and let f : E → Y be a continuous map that is holomorphic on a neighbourhood U of A
and admits a product spray with core f |U that is dominating over U \ A. Then, for every
r ≥ 1, there exists a holomorphic map f˜: E → Y that agrees with f to order r along A.
20                             Y. KUSAKABE AND S. MATSUMURA


   Theorem 1.4 is deduced from Theorem 3.1 in Section 4.
   Strategy of the proof of Theorem 3.1. We follow the proof of the Oka principle for Stein
sources [8, Chap. 5]. We exhaust the total space E by the disc bundles {θw < 1} defined
below, and we pass from one disc bundle to a larger one in finitely many steps, each of
which attaches a convex bump V to a set U ⊃ A (Lemma 3.13). At each step, the current
map F is holomorphic on U , and on the convex set V the Oka property of Y provides a
holomorphic map G that approximates F on U ∩ V . To glue F and G, we use dominating
product sprays H with core F and T with core G. Near U ∩ V , the old spray can be
written as H = T ◦ γ, where γ(x, ·) is close to the identity map of the parameter space
(Lemma 3.15). If γ = β ◦ α−1 with α defined over U and β over V , then H ◦ α and
T ◦ β agree on U ∩ V and together form a product spray over U ∪ V (Lemma 3.16). This
compositional splitting is a nonlinear version of the additive Cousin problem c = b − a,
from which it is obtained by iteration (Lemma 3.7); the additive problem is solved via
the ∂-equation (Lemma 3.6). Here U contains A and need not be compact or Stein, so
we solve the ∂-equation with L2 estimates for a weight q −m that is singular along A;
this weight also forces α to agree with the identity to order r along A, which yields the
interpolation along A. Since the disc bundles are not compact, we also need bounds near
the ends of X (Lemmas 3.5 and 3.10). Finally, the functions θw have no critical points off
A (Lemma 3.2(d)); hence, unlike in the Stein case, no handles need to be attached.

Lemma 3.6 (Additive splitting). Let m ≥ max{c+1, N +r−1}, and let D = DA ∪DB ⊂ E
be weakly pseudoconvex, where DA , DB are open, DB is compact and disjoint from A, and
DC = DA ∩DB . Let χ ∈ C ∞ (E, [0, 1]) satisfy χ = 0 near DA \DB and χ = 1 near DB \DA ,
and assume that supp dχ is compact, disjoint from A, and satisfies supp dχ ∩ D ⊂ DC .
For a bounded holomorphic map c : DC → Ck , let vc be the minimal solution of ∂v = c ∂χ
on D, and put ac = vc − χc on DA and bc = vc + (1 − χ)c on DB . Then ac and bc are
holomorphic, bc − ac = c, ac vanishes to order r along A, and
           ∥ac ∥DA + ∥bc ∥DB ≤ C0 sup |c|, C0 = 2 µm (DB )1/2 + 2 ∥∂χ∥D ,
                  R
where µm (DB ) = DB dµm < ∞. Moreover, holomorphic dependence on parameters is
preserved.
Proof. The form c ∂χ on D, extended by 0, is smooth and ∂-closed, since supp dχ ∩ D ⊂
DC . Its norm is at most sup |c| ∥∂χ∥D , which is finite because supp dχ is compact and
disjoint from A, so that q is bounded below on it. Similarly, χc and (1 − χ)c extend
from DC to DA and to DB , respectively, and are supported in DB , so their norms are at
most sup |c| µm (DB )1/2 ; here µm (DB ) < ∞ because DB is compact and disjoint from A.
Lemma 3.3 gives ∥vc ∥D ≤ ∥c ∂χ∥D , and the estimate follows. Near A, we have ac = vc , so
ac vanishes to order r along A by Lemma 3.4. The minimal solution depends linearly and
boundedly on the data, which gives holomorphic dependence on parameters.               □
   The next lemma is the analogue of the splitting lemma [8, Proposition 5.8.1] (a gener-
alization of Cartan’s lemma on invertible matrices) and of [20, Theorem 5.2]. It is purely
formal: the geometry enters only through the hypothesis on additive splittings, which is
verified for the pairs (Uλ , Vλ ) in Lemma 3.14. Since the weighted L2 estimates give supre-
mum bounds only on slightly smaller sets, we replace the implicit function theorem on a
fixed Banach space used in [8, 20] by a Newton iteration on shrinking domains.

     For T ≥ 1, we consider functions r on E satisfying

Definition 3.11. A convex bump consists of smooth psh functions rD ≤ rU on E satisfying
(17), with rD ≥ −2, rU = −1 on A, and {rD ≤ 1} ∩ π −1 (K) compact for every compact
set K ⊂ X, together with a chart z : Ω → {|z| < 3}, where Ω ⊂ π −1 ({ρ < T + 1}) \ A,
in which rU , rD are strictly convex, such that rU = rD outside {|z| < 1}. For 0 < λ ≤ 41 ,
put Uλ = {rU < λ}, Dλ = {rD < λ}, Vλ = Dλ ∩ {|z|2 < 4 + λ} and Cλ = Uλ ∩ Vλ , and
define χΩ = h(|z|2 ) on Ω and χΩ = 0 on E \ Ω, where h ∈ C ∞ (R, [0, 1]) satisfies h = 1 on
(−∞, 1] and h = 0 on [2, ∞).

   The pair (Uλ , Vλ ) plays the role of a Cartan pair [8, Definition 5.7.1] or of a 1-convex
Cartan pair [20, Definition 5.1]. Of the defining properties of a Cartan pair, we use only
the separation property (Lemma 3.12(c)), which gives the cut-off function in the additive
splitting, and the convexity of Vλ and Cλ (Lemma 3.12(a)), which is needed for approxima-
tion and for transition maps. The Stein property of Dλ , which in [8, Lemma 5.8.2] yields
solutions of the ∂-equation with bounds, is replaced by the weak pseudoconvexity of Dλ
(Lemma 3.12(b)) and the weighted L2 estimates of Lemma 3.3; as in [20, Proposition 4.5],
the ∂-data are supported away from A.
                     ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                                  25


Lemma 3.12.       (a) Dλ = Uλ ∪ Vλ ; Vλ and Cλ = Uλ ∩ {|z|2 < 4 + λ} are convex in the
      chart; Vλ ⊂ Ω is compact.
  (b) Uλ and Dλ are weakly pseudoconvex.
  (c) On Dλ : {χΩ < 1} ⊂ Uλ , {χΩ > 0} ⊂ Vλ , supp dχΩ ⊂ Cλ .
  (d) There exists c1 > 0 such that, for λ′ < λ, the sets Vλ′ and Uλ′ ∩ π −1 ({ρ ≤ T + 1})
      have distance ≥ c1 (λ − λ′ ) from E \ Vλ and E \ Uλ .

Proof. Assertions (a) and (c) follow since rD < rU only in {|z| < 1} and supp dχΩ ⊂
{1 ≤ |z|2 ≤ 2}. For (b), use − log(λ − r) + Ψ as in Lemma 3.2(b). For (d), bound
|drU |, |drD |, |d|z|2 | on a neighbourhood of the compact set ({rD ≤ 1} ∩ π −1 ({ρ ≤ T +
1})) ∪ {|z|2 ≤ 17  4 }.                                                                 □

Lemma 3.13 (Decomposition into convex bumps). Let T ≥ 1, let w ≥ w′ be smooth psh
functions on X with w = w′ = χ◦ρ on {ρ ≥ T }, put rs = θ(1−s)w+sw′ −1, and let 0 < ϵ ≤ 41 .
                                (i) (i)
Then there exist convex bumps (rU , rD ), i = 1, . . . , I, with charts in {θw > 1 − 2ϵ}, such
           (i)   (i)
that r1 ≤ rD ≤ rU ≤ r0 and, for |λ| ≤ ϵ/2,
          (1)                              (i)         (i+1)             (I)
       {rU < λ} = {r0 < λ},           {rD < λ} = {rU           < λ},   {rD < λ} = {r1 < λ}.

Proof. This is the usual construction for noncritical strongly psh exhaustion functions [8,
Lemma 5.10.3], carried out over {ρ ≤ T }. By Lemma 3.2, the functions rs are psh on E,
strictly psh and without critical points on E \ A, equal to −1 on A, and independent of s
                                                     ′
over {ρ ≥ T }. Since rs + 1 = q e((1−s)w+sw )◦π and w′ ≤ w, they are nonincreasing in s,
and rs′ → rs in C 2 on compact sets as s′ → s. (They are not affine in s; only log(rs + 1)
is.)
    Charts. The set Z of pairs (s, x) ∈ [0, 1]×E with ρ(π(x)) ≤ T and |rs (x)| ≤ ϵ is compact
and does not meet [0, 1] × A. By Narasimhan’s lemma, for every (s∗ , x∗ ) ∈ Z there exist a
chart z : Ω → {|z| < 3} centred at x∗ , with Ω ⊂ {θw > 1 − 2ϵ} ∩ π −1 ({ρ < T + 1}) \ A, and
a number δ > 0 such that rs is strictly convex in z near Ω for |s − s∗ | < 2δ. Finitely many
of the sets (s∗ − δ, s∗ + δ) × {|z| < 1} cover Z; let δ0 be the smallest of the corresponding δ.
Cover [0, 1] by closed intervals I1 , . . . , Ip of length < δ0 . For each a, let Ωa,1 , . . . , Ωa,Ka be
the charts of this cover whose interval meets Ia . Then rs is strictly convex near each Ωa,k for
s ∈ Ia , and the balls {|z| < 1} of these charts cover Ma = {x : (s, x) ∈ Z for some s ∈ Ia }.
                                                                                  P
Choose smooth functions χa,k ≥ 0 supported in these balls such that k χa,k ≤ 1, with
equality near Ma .
    Bumps. Since there are only finitely many functions χa,k and rs′ → rs in C 2 on compact
sets as s′ → s, there exists a subdivision 0 = s0 < s1 < · · · < sL = 1 such that each
[sl , sl+1 ] lies in some Ia(l) and the functions
                                    X                      
                       rl,k = rsl +    χa(l),k′ rsl+1 − rsl ,      0 ≤ k ≤ Ka(l) ,
                                   k′ ≤k

are so close to rsl in C 2 on k Ωa(l),k that they are strictly convex on each Ωa(l),k . Outside
                               S

these charts, rl,k = rsl ; hence rl,k is psh on E. At each point, rl,k is a convex combination of
rsl and rsl+1 , so r1 ≤ rl,k ≤ r0 , rl,k = −1 on A, and (17) holds. The difference rl,k−1 −rl,k ≥
26                              Y. KUSAKABE AND S. MATSUMURA


0 is supported in the ball {|z| < 1} of Ωa(l),k . Therefore the pairs (rU , rD ) = (rl,k−1 , rl,k ),
1 ≤ k ≤ Ka(l) , with the charts Ωa(l),k , ordered lexicographically in (l, k), are convex bumps.
   Matching. Consecutive bumps with the same l share a function, and r0,0 = r0 . It
remains to compare rl,K , where K = Ka(l) , with rl+1,0 = rsl+1 . They agree near Ma(l) and
over {ρ > T }. At any other point x, we have |rs (x)| > ϵ for all s ∈ [sl , sl+1 ], so rsl (x) and
rsl+1 (x) have the same sign and absolute values > ϵ, and rl,K (x) lies between them. Hence
{rl,K < λ} = {rsl+1 < λ} for |λ| ≤ ϵ/2.                                                          □

Lemma 3.14 (Splitting over a convex bump). Let (rU , rD ) be a convex bump, let 41 ≥
λ+ > λ− > 0, and let B0 , B∞ ⊂ Ck be balls centred at 0 with radii ρ0 > ρ∞ . Then there
exist ϵ∗ , C ′ > 0 such that, for every holomorphic map γ on Cλ+ × B0 with sup |γ − ζ| ≤ ϵ∗ ,
there exist holomorphic maps α : Uλ− × B∞ → B0 and β : Vλ− × B∞ → Ck such that
γ(x, α(x, ζ)) = β(x, ζ) on Cλ− × B∞ , sup |α − ζ| + sup |β − ζ| ≤ C ′ sup |γ − ζ|, and
α(·, ζ) − ζ vanishes to order r along A.

Proof. Let λj = λ− + (λ+ − λ− )2−j . We verify the hypothesis of Lemma 3.7 for the
sets Uλj , Vλj with p = nE . Applying Lemma 3.6 on Dλj with DA = Uλj , DB = Vλj
and the cut-off function χΩ (Lemma 3.12), we split c with L2 norms ≤ C0 sup |c|, where
C0 = 2µm (Vλ+ )1/2 + 2∥∂χΩ ∥E does not depend on j since Vλj ⊂ Vλ+ and Vλ+ is a compact
subset of Ω ⊂ E \ A. On Vλj+1 and on Uλj+1 ∩ π −1 ({ρ ≤ T + 1}), the mean value
inequality on balls of radius c1 (λj − λj+1 ) (Lemma 3.12(d)) gives sup bounds of the form
O(2nE j ) sup |c|. At a point ξ ∈ Uλj+1 with ρ(π(ξ)) ≥ T + 1, we have Uλj = WRj near ξ,
where Rj = (1 + λj )1/2 e−χ(ρ◦π)/2 , as well as ξ ∈ W(1−δj )Rj with δj ≥ (λj − λj+1 )/4 and
q(ξ) ≤ 1. Lemma 3.10(b) gives Λ with B(ξ, 2/Λ) ⊂ π −1 ({ρ ≥ T }), and Lemma 3.5, with
m − nE ≥ 1, then gives |ac (ξ)| ≤ C0 δj−nE sup |c|.                                       □

Gluing. Let Y be an Oka manifold with a complete Riemannian metric, and let Ps ⊂ CM
denote the ball of radius s. We use the basic Oka property with approximation for maps
from Stein manifolds to Y [8, Corollary 5.4.5], the polynomial convexity of compact convex
sets [12], the existence of dominating sprays over holomorphic maps from Stein manifolds
[8, Lemma 5.10.4], and the homotopy extension property of (E, {r ≤ λ}) for regular values
λ. As in [8, Sects. 5.9–5.10] and [20, Sects. 6 and 8], we first glue two sprays over a pair
(Uλ , Vλ ) and then extend across a convex bump.

Lemma 3.15 (Transition maps; [8, Lemma 5.9.3], [20, Lemma 6.2]). Let S be a Stein
manifold, let G : S × P1 → Y be a holomorphic map such that ∂ζ G is surjective everywhere,
let L ⊂ S be compact, and let L1 be a compact neighbourhood of L. Then, for every ϵ1 ∈
    1
(0, 16 ], there exist a neighbourhood W of L and δ1 > 0 with the following property: for every
k and every holomorphic map T defined near L1 ×P3/4 ×Bk with dist(T (x, ζ, w), G(x, ζ)) <
δ1 there, there exists a holomorphic map γζ : W × P1/4 × Bk → P1/2 such that |γζ − ζ| < ϵ1
and T (x, γζ (x, ζ, w), w) = G(x, ζ).

Proof. We follow [8, p. 240], keeping track of the parameter domain. Let Π be a holomor-
phic right inverse of ∂ζ G, which exists by Theorem B. By the inverse function theorem,
v 7→ G(x, ζ + Πv) has a local inverse y 7→ v(x, ζ, y) near G(x, ζ), uniformly for (x, ζ) near
                   ATIYAH CLASSES AND ELLIPTICITY OF OKA MANIFOLDS                             27


L × P1/2 . For sufficiently small δ1 , independent of k and T , the map η = ζ + Πv(x, ζ, T )
satisfies T = G(x, η) and |η − ζ| < ϵ1 ; solving η(x, γζ , w) = ζ ′ by the contraction principle
on B(ζ ′ , 2ϵ1 ) (using the Cauchy estimates) gives γζ .                                      □

Lemma 3.16 (Gluing lemma; cf. [8, Proposition 5.9.2], [20, Proposition 6.1]). Let (rU , rD )
be a convex bump, let 14 ≥ λ1 > λ+ > λ− > 0 and k ≥ 0, and let H : Uλ1 × P1 → Y be a
product spray that is dominating over Uλ1 \ A. Then, for every ε′ > 0, there exists δ ′ > 0
with the following property. Let T be a holomorphic map from a neighbourhood of Vλ+ ×
P3/4 × Bk to Y such that ∂(ζ,w) T is surjective everywhere and dist(T (x, ζ, w), H(x, ζ)) < δ ′
on Cλ+ ×P3/4 ×Bk . Then there exist holomorphic maps α = (αζ , αw ) : Uλ− ×P ′ → P1/2 ×Bk
and β : Vλ− ×P ′ → P1/2 ×Bk , where P ′ ⊂ CM +k is the ball of radius 16
                                                                      1
                                                                         , such that α(·, v)−v
                                                             ′
vanishes to order r along A, |α(x, v) − v|, |β(x, v) − v| < ε , and

    H ′ (x, v) = H(x, αζ (x, v)) on Uλ− × P ′ ,     H ′ (x, v) = T (x, β(x, v)) on Vλ− × P ′

define a product spray H ′ : Dλ− × P ′ → Y that is dominating over Dλ− \ A.

Proof. Choose λ′ ∈ (λ− , λ+ ). Let ϵ∗ , C ′ be the constants of Lemma 3.14 for the levels
λ′ > λ− and the balls of radii 41 , 81 in CM +k , and put ϵ1 = min{ϵ∗ , 1/(32C ′ ), ε′ /(2C ′ )}.
Applying Lemma 3.15 to G = H on the convex domain S = Cλ1 , which does not meet A,
with L = Cλ′ and L1 = Cλ+ , we obtain W and δ ′ = δ1 . Then γ(x, v) = (γζ (x, v), w), where
v = (ζ, w), is defined on W × P1/4 × Bk , satisfies |γ − v| < ϵ1 , and T (x, γ(x, v)) = H(x, ζ).
Lemma 3.14 gives α on Uλ− and β on Vλ− such that γ ◦α = β on Cλ− , sup |α−v|+sup |β −
v| ≤ C ′ ϵ1 , and α(·, v) − v vanishes to order r along A. By the Cauchy estimates, ∂v α and
∂v β are within 21 of the identity on P ′ . On Cλ− × P ′ , we have T ◦ β = T ◦ γ ◦ α = H(x, αζ ),
so H ′ is well defined; it is dominating by the chain rule, since H is dominating over Uλ1 \ A
and T is dominating.                                                                           □

Lemma 3.17 (Extension across a convex bump; cf. [8, Lemma 5.10.5], [20, Proposi-
tion 8.3]). Let (rU , rD ) be a convex bump, let 0 < λ0 < λ1 ≤ 41 , where λ0 is a regular value
of rD , let F : E → Y be a continuous map, and let H : Uλ1 × P → Y be a product spray
with core F |Uλ1 that is dominating over Uλ1 \ A. Let K ⊂ {rU < 0} be compact and ε > 0.
Then there exist a continuous map F ′ : E → Y that agrees with F to order r along A and
satisfies dist(F ′ , F ) < ε on K, and a product spray H ′ : Dλ0 × P ′ → Y , P ′ ⊂ CM +dim Y ,
with core F ′ |Dλ0 that is dominating over Dλ0 \ A.

Proof. We may assume that P = P1 . Put k = dim Y , choose λ1 > λ2 > λ3 > λ0 , and put
V ′ = Vλ1 . The sets KU = Cλ2 ⊂ KV = Vλ2 are compact and convex in V ′ (Lemma 3.12(a)),
and Vλ3 ⊂ KV .
   Tolerances. Let 2δ be less than the convexity radius of Y near F (KU ). Choose ε′ > 0
such that dist(H(x, ζ), F (x)) < min{δ/2, ε} for x ∈ KU ∪ K and |ζ| < ε′ , let δ ′ be the
constant given by Lemma 3.16 for λ1 > λ2 > λ3 , k and ε′ , and put δ1 = min{δ ′ , δ/2}.
   Approximation. Let Ĥ(x, ζ) = H(x, ψ(x)ζ), where ψ ∈ Cc∞ (Uλ1 ∩V ′ ) satisfies 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 1
and equals 1 near KU (so that ψ(x)ζ ∈ P1 for ζ ∈ P1 ), and let Ĥ = F elsewhere on
V ′ × P1 . The set KU × P7/8 is compact and convex, hence O(V ′ × P1 )-convex. The basic
28                             Y. KUSAKABE AND S. MATSUMURA


Oka property gives a homotopy Ĥt from Ĥ to a holomorphic map G on V ′ × P1 such that
Ĥt is holomorphic near KU × P7/8 and satisfies dist(Ĥt , H) < δ1 /2 there; put gt = Ĥt (·, 0).
    Thickening. We apply [8, Lemma 5.10.4] to the section (x, ζ) 7→ ((x, ζ), G(x, ζ)) of
(V ′ × P1 ) × Y → V ′ × P1 and the compact convex set KV × P3/4 . Since this set has
contractible Stein neighbourhoods, the lemma gives a spray Ĝ(x, ζ, w), with w near 0 ∈ Ck ,
such that Ĝ(x, ζ, 0) = G(x, ζ) and ∂w Ĝ is surjective near KV × P3/4 × {0}. For sufficiently
small σ > 0, the map T (x, ζ, w) = Ĝ(x, ζ, σw) is defined near KV × P3/4 × Bk , ∂w T is
surjective there, and dist(T, H) < δ1 on KU × P3/4 × Bk .
    Gluing. Lemma 3.16 with λ+ = λ2 and λ− = λ3 gives α, β and a spray H ′′ over Dλ3
that is dominating off A. Its core is f ′ = H(x, a(x)) on Uλ3 , where a = αζ (·, 0), and

                                  1

The approximation theorem. The sublevel set {θw < c} is the disc bundle {|ξ| < R(π(ξ))},
whose radius R is determined by q(R) = c e−w . The following approximation theorem
                                                 ′
enlarges the radius from about e−w/2 to about e−w /2 ; it combines Lemmas 3.13 and 3.17
and corresponds to [8, Proposition 5.10.1].

admits a product spray with core F ′ |W ′ that is dominating over W ′ \ A, agrees with F to
order r along A, and satisfies dist(F ′ , F ) < ε on K.

                                                (i)

Proof of Theorem 3.1. We may assume that r ≥ 2 and nE + r − 1 ≥ c + 1. Let wj = φj ◦ ρ
(Lemma 3.19); then wj ≥ wj+1 and wj = wj+1 = χ ◦ ρ on {ρ ≥ tj+1 }. By Lemma 3.10(a),

and ε = 2−j , we obtain continuous maps Fj : E → Y with F0 = f that are holomorphic
on {θwj < 1 + ℓj } ⊃ Lj , agree with f to order r along A, and satisfy dist(Fj+1 , Fj ) < 2−j
on Lj . Since every compact subset of E lies in some Lj , the maps Fj converge locally
uniformly to a holomorphic map f˜: E → Y , which agrees with f to order r along A by
the Cauchy estimates.                                                                      □

                          4. Proof of Gromov’s conjecture
  In this section, we first apply Corollary 2.7 to weakly pseudoconvex manifolds admitting
a positive line bundle, and then prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.4.
Theorem 4.1. Let X be a weakly pseudoconvex complex manifold admitting a positive line
bundle. Then X admits a local dominating spray.
Proof of Theorem 4.1. By Takayama’s embedding theorem [21], there exists an embedding
ι : X ,→ PN , which is not necessarily proper. Set
                        H := ι∗ OPN (1) and B := KX ⊗ H ⊗(2n+1) ,
where n := dim X. We use the following claim.
Claim 4.2. The line bundle B = KX ⊗ H ⊗(2n+1) has the following properties:
    • B is positive.
    • B is generated by finitely many sections.
    • Finitely many sections of B define an embedding of X into a projective space.
    • TX ⊗ B is generated by finitely many sections.
Proof of Claim 4.2. Since ι : X ,→ PN is an embedding, H is positive and generated by
finitely many sections. The natural surjection ι∗ ΩP1N → ΩX 1 induces a surjective bundle

Proof of Theorem 1.1. Let H, B = KX ⊗ H ⊗(2n+1) and E = (B ∨ )⊕m be as in the proof of

  Since KX −1
              ⊗B ∼= H ⊗(2n+1) admits a metric with semipositive curvature, induced by
the Fubini–Study metric, Theorem 1.4, applied with k = 1 and N = m, shows that
E = (B ∨ )⊕m admits a dominating spray.                                                 □
Corollary 4.3. Stein Oka manifolds and projective Oka manifolds are elliptic.
Proof. A Stein manifold is weakly pseudoconvex, and the trivial line bundle with the metric
e−ψ , for a smooth strictly psh exhaustion function ψ, is positive. A projective manifold is
compact, hence weakly pseudoconvex, and it has a positive line bundle. A point is elliptic.
Hence Theorem 1.1 applies.                                                                □
  Both statements are known: the Stein case is classical [8, Chap. 5], and the projective
case is due to Forstnerič and Lárusson [10].
